abstract: Abstract Root metabolites and soil microbial community structure in the rhizosphere play critical roles in crop growth. Here, we assessed the efficiency of conventional and tissue culture propagation methods in modulating the soil health and microbiota in the rhizosphere of sugarcane ( Saccharum officinarum L.) plants. The seeding canes were obtained using newly planted and two‐year ratooned canes propagated by conventional (CSN and CSR) or tissue culture (TCN and TCR) methods. Changes in soil fertility, root metabolites and soil microbial community structure in the rhizosphere of sugarcane plants obtained using these canes were assessed. The activities of soil β ‐glucosidase and aminopeptidase, soil microbial biomass nitrogen, and abundances of soil beneficial microbes, both at phyla and genera levels, were significantly higher in the rhizosphere of sugarcane plants in TCN and TCR treatments than those in that of plants in CSN and CSR treatments. Furthermore, flavonoid and flavonol biosynthesis and alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism were significantly upregulated in the roots of TCR and TCN plants compared with those in the roots of CSN and CSR plants. These results suggest that the tissue culture propagation method is a sustainable method for sugarcane cultivation to improve soil fertility and health in sugarcane rhizosphere.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE
Study site, experimental design and management
The experiments were conducted at the Experimental Base of Fusui, Chongzuo City, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China (107°55′4″ E, 22°44′56″ N). This location is in a subtropical monsoon climate zone with ample heat, rainfall and sunshine. The average annual temperature and precipitation are approximately 22°C and 1273.6 mm, respectively. The soil type of the experimental site was acidic red loam with the following chemical properties: pH, 5.8; organic matter content, 23.3 g/kg; total nitrogen, 1.7 g/kg; phosphorus, 0.4 g/kg; potassium, 2.7 g/kg. The available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium were 48.7, 12.4 and 66.1 mg/kg, respectively.
Newly planted and ratoon canes (two‐year ratooning) of the “Zhong Tang 3” cultivar were planted in March 2022 and March 2021, respectively. Depending on the method of propagation and types of planting materials used, we designed five treatments as follows: newly planted canes propagated using tissue culture (TCN); newly planted canes propagated using conventional (stem) propagation method (CSN); ratoon canes propagated using tissue culture (TCR); ratoon canes propagated using conventional (stem) propagation method (CSR:); and a barren plot with no sugarcane planting used as a rhizosphere soil control (background, BG).

Root and rhizosphere soil sample collection
Rhizospheric soil samples were randomly collected from the sugarcane cultivation area in November 2022 using the shaking‐off method (Riley & Barber,
1970
). Briefly, three sugarcane plants were selected randomly from each plot. The soil around each plant (~ 60 cm in diameter) was loosened using a sterile shovel. The base of each plant was then held, and the entire plant, along with the surrounding soil, was manually pulled out. The soil adhering to the roots was carefully collected in a sterile sealed bag and placed in a box with ice packs. Additionally, soil samples from the same experimental area without growing sugarcane were randomly collected as BG samples. All samples were transferred to the laboratory as soon as possible and shifted using a 2 mm stainless steel sieve to remove the impurities, like small stones and leaf debris. The shifted material was then stored at −80°C.
Root samples were rinsed with sterile water to remove the soil and attached appendages from the surface. After rinsing, the samples were blotted dry using a sterile filter paper.
Evaluation of soil biological properties
To evaluate the biological properties of soil, we assessed the activities of β‐glucosidase, aminopeptidase, and acid phosphatase using the method described in previous studies (Hayano,
1973
; Ladd,
1972
; Yang et al.,
2021
, respectively). The soil microbial biomass carbon (MBC) and nitrogen were measured using chloroform fumigation and extraction techniques (Brookes et al.,
1985
; Vance et al.,
1987

1987
).
Soil microbial diversity analysis
Total DNA was extracted from soil samples using the E.Z.N.A.® Soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio‐tek, Norcross, GA, USA) following the manufacturer's instructions. The integrity of extracted DNA was checked using 1% agarose gel and quantified using a NanoDrop 2000 UV–Vis spectrophotometer (Thermal Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The fungal internal transcribed spacer 1 region was amplified using an ABIGeneAmp® 9700 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) thermal cycler (Applied Biosystems, CA, USA). PCR products were resolved using 2% agar‐gel electrophoresis, purified using the AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (Axygen, USA), and quantified using a quantitative fluorometer (Promega, USA). PCR amplification and sequencing of total DNA extracted from the inter‐root soil samples were performed by Meguiar Biotechnology Ltd. LC–MS
‐based soil untargeted metabolomics
The sample (20 mg) was placed in a 2 mL centrifuge tube containing a grinding bead (diameter of 6 mm) and 400 μL of extraction solution (methanol: water = 4:1 [v:v]) containing 0.02 mg/mL of internal standard (L‐2‐chlorophenylalanine) was added for metabolite extraction. The sample solution was then ground for 6 min (−10°C, 50 Hz) in a frozen tissue mill, followed by 30 min of low‐temperature sonication (5°C, 40 kHz). The samples were left at −20°C for 30 min, centrifuged for 15 min (4°C, 13,000 ×
g
), and the supernatant was transferred to an injection vial with an internal cannula for LC–MS analysis. The LC–MS analysis was performed using an ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography‐tandem Fourier transform mass spectrometry system (UHPLC‐Q Exactive, Thermo Fisher Scientific) fitted with an HSS T3 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm; internal diameter, 1.8 μm). The chromatographic conditions were as follows: injection volume, 2 μL; mobile phase A, 95% water +5% acetonitrile (containing 0.1% formic acid); mobile phase B, 47.5% acetonitrile, 47.5% isopropanol, and 5% water (containing 0.1% formic acid); separation gradient: 0–0.1 min, mobile phase B increased from linear 0% to 5%; 0.1–2 min, mobile phase B increased from linear 5% to 25%; 2–9 min, mobile phase B linearity increased from 25% to 100%; 9–13 min, mobile phase B linearity maintained 100%; 13.0–13.1 min, mobile phase B linearity decreased from 100% to 0%; 13.1–29.1 min, the linearity of mobile phase B was maintained at 0% for 16 min; flow rate, 0.40 mL/min; and column temperature, 40°C.
Statistical analysis
Test data were statistically analysed using Microsoft Excel 2019 and SPSS 21.0. The results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation of the mean. The alpha diversity of the bacterial and fungal communities were calculated using Mothur (version 1.30.2,

For the analysis of microbial community composition and Venn diagrams, OTU tables with 97% similarity were selected and analysed using the R language (version 3.3.1) tool. The pre‐processed metabolite data matrix was subjected to principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS‐DA) using the ‘ropls’ package in R (version 1.6.2). Soil bacterial community structure in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under different propagation methods
Soil microbes are crucial in the relationship between plants and the soil. They significantly impact plant growth, productivity, nutrient availability and ecosystem functions (Li et al.,
2019
; Bonkowski & Roy,
2005
). In the newly planted treatments, the Shannon indices of soil bacteria in the sugarcane rhizospheres were not significantly different between TCN and CSN. However, the Ace indices of the soil bacteria in the TCN treatment were significantly higher than those in the CSN and BG treatments (Figure
1A,B
). Significant differences in the soil bacterial composition were detected between the TCN and CSN treatments in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants (Figure
1C
). The numbers of soil bacteria at the OTU level in the TCN, CSN and BG treatments were 3244, 2931 and 2953, respectively. The numbers of unique bacteria in these three treatments were 501, 337 and 351, respectively (Figure
S1A
).

In the ratoon cane treatments, the Shannon indices of soil bacteria in the rhizosphere of sugarcane in TCR treatments were significantly higher than those of CSR treatments (Figure
1D
). Moreover, their compositions in TCR, CSR and BG treatments clustered separately (Figure
1D–F
). At the OTU level, the total and unique numbers of soil bacteria in the TCR (3424, 486), CSR (2852, 359) and BG (2953, 318) treatments showed considerable differences (Figure
S1B
). Together, these results suggest the advantages of the tissue culture propagation method on the soil bacterial community structure in the rhizosphere of sugarcane.
Soil microbes play key regulatory roles in suppressing soil‐borne diseases and promoting plant growth (Mendes et al.,
2011
). Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, Acidobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Myxococcus and Patescibacteria were the dominant bacterial phyla in the rhizospheres of sugarcane in the TCN and CSN treatments. Among these, the abundances of Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes and Myxococcus were higher in the TCN treatment than those in the CSN treatment (Figure
2A
). Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LefSe) analysis also showed that Bacteroidetes were significantly enriched in TCN treatment (
p
< 0.05; Figure
S2A
). In addition, Gemmatimonadota and Verrucomicrobiota were the predominant bacterial phyla in the TCN group. Actinobacteria can produce spores in response to harsh environments (Boer et al.,
2005
) and are positively associated with plant residue decomposition, inorganic nitrogen fixation, soil aggregate formation, and plant disease resistance (Zhao et al.,
2016
). An increased abundance of Bacteroidetes indicates high‐quality soil (Kruczyńska et al.,
2023
). Myxococcota are widely distributed in agricultural soils and are important in regulating soil microbial community structure and ecosystem functions (Mohr,
2018
; Wang et al.,
2020
).

Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, Acidobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Myxococcus, Gemmatimonadota, Patescibacteria, Verrucomicrobiota and Planctomycetota were also identified as dominant bacterial phyla in the rhizospheres of sugarcane in TCR and CSR (Figure
2C
). Compared with the CSR treatment, the proportions of Chloroflexi and Acidobacteria increased with the TCR treatment. Firmicutes, Nitrospirota and Cyanobacteria were the dominant soil bacterial phyla in the rhizosphere of sugarcane under the TCR treatment. Acidobacteria can produce secondary metabolites and antibacterial compounds (Parsley et al.,
2011
; Ward et al.,
2009

2011
). Nitrospirota suppresses the growth of some disease‐causing fungi, such as
Fusarium graminearum
in wheat and
Fusarium acnes
in strawberries and bananas (Cha et al.,
2016
; Sanguin et al.,
2009
). Moreover, Nitrospirota plays a crucial role in nitrification and nitrogen cycling and helps plant growth (Zhang et al.,
2018
). Cyanobacteria provide organic matter and oxygen to their hosts via biological nitrogen fixation and photosynthesis (Gavazov et al.,
2010
; Zhang, Zhang, et al.,
2011
).

Bradyrhizobium
is a gram‐negative bacteria widely distributed in the soil that forms nodules in plant roots and promotes plant growth and development by fixing atmospheric nitrogen (Favero et al.,
2022
). In addition,
Bradyrhizobium
has a significant inhibitory effect on the growth of pathogenic fungi in the soil, which can reduce the incidence of crop diseases (Basile & Lepek,
2021
).
Sphingomonas
, a group of gram‐negative bacteria, is involved in phosphorus solubilisation functions, degrades soil organic pollutants, and reduces soil toxicity (Li et al.,
2017
).
Streptomyces
is a phosphate‐solubilising soil microorganism that mediates the solubilisation and mineralisation of soil‐insoluble phosphate to a bioavailable form for plants (Abo‐Zai et al.,
2020
). Previous studies have confirmed the efficacy of
Streptomyces
as biofertilisers to improve soil health, reduce barriers to plant succession, and increase plant productivity (Ali et al.,
2021
; Pang et al.,
2022
; Prigigallo et al.,
2023
). Additionally, It can establish a good synergy with
Trichoderma

2020
; Ezziyyani et al.,
2007
).
Similarly, the numbers of soil‐dominant bacterial genera obtained from TCR, CSR and BG treatments were 26, 19 and 22, respectively (Figure

). Compared with the CSR treatment, the abundances of
Conexibacter
and
Sinomonas
were enriched in the TCR treatment (
p
< 0.05; Figure

).
Conexibacter
enhances the resistance of the inter‐root microzone to ecotoxicity and improves microbial community stability in heavy metal‐contaminated soils (Chen et al.,
2022
).
These results indicate that different propagation methods could significantly alter the soil bacterial community composition in the rhizosphere of sugarcane in both newly planted and ratooning systems and that the tissue culture propagation methods recruit more beneficial rhizosphere microorganisms than conventional propagation methods.

Soil fungal community structure in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under different propagation methods
The Shannon indices of soil fungi in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants under TCN treatment were significantly higher than those under CSN and BG treatments. However, no significant difference was observed in the Ace indices of the soil fungi between the TCN and CSN treatments (Figure
3A,B
). Soil fungal composition in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants differed significantly between TCN and CSN treatments (Figure
3C
). The total numbers of soil fungi at the OTU level in the TCN, CSN and BG treatments were 1502, 1324 and 1190, respectively, and those of unique soil fungi were 528, 325 and 278, respectively (Figure
S2A
).

In the ratoon cane treatments, the Shannon indices of soil fungi in the rhizosphere of sugarcane were significantly higher in the TCR treatment than those in the CSR treatment. The Ace and Chao indices of soil fungi were also significantly higher in the TCR and CSR treatments than those in the BG treatment; however, they did not differ significantly between the TCR and CSR treatments (Figure
3D,E
). Moreover, PCA of soil fungal compositions in the rhizosphere of sugarcane plants revealed different clusters in the TCR, CSR and BG treatments (Figure
3F
). This result suggests significant differences in the soil fungal community structure between the TCR and CSR treatments. The numbers of soil fungi obtained in the TCR, CSR and BG treatments at the OTU level were 1502, 1324 and 1190, respectively, whereas those of specific soil fungi were 528, 325 and 278, respectively (Figure
S2B
). Together, these results indicate that compared to conventional propagation, tissue culture propagation can significantly increase the diversity of soil fungi in the rhizosphere of sugarcane.
At the phylum level, Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, unclassified_k_fungi, and Mortierellomycota were the dominant phyla in the rhizospheres of sugarcane under the TCN and CSN treatments (Figure
4A
). Ascomycota was the most abundant fungal phylum in both the TCN and CSN treatments, accounting for 77.36% and 70.83%, respectively. Meanwhile, compared with the CSN treatment, the abundance of Basidiomycota and unclassified_k_Fungi decreased, and that of Mortierellomycota increased in the TCN treatment. Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, unclassified Fungi, and Mortierellomycota were also identified as the dominant fungal phyla in the rhizosphere of sugarcane in TCR and CSR treatments. Among these, the abundance of Mortierellomycota in the TCR treatment was higher in the rhizospheres of sugarcane than that in the CSR treatment (Figure

). Ascomycota is one of the most abundant fungal phyla in soil (Egidi et al.,

2013

2020
; Zhang, Wu, et al.,
2011
). Mortierella participates in the degradation of plant residues and effectively contributes to the soil carbon cycle (Takashi,
2005

Profile of metabolites in rhizosphere of sugarcane plants under different propagation methods
Metabolomics aims to analyse the metabolome of an organism at a specific time under specific conditions and it is considered the chemical phenotype of an organism. In this study, 177 and 147 significantly differentially expressed metabolites (
p
< 0.05, VIP >2) were identified between the two treatments using newly planted (TCN vs. CSN) and ratoon canes (TCR vs. CSR), respectively. The differential metabolites between newly planted canes (TCN vs. CSN) were grouped into eight classes: phenylpropanoids and polyketides (29.07%), organic oxygen compounds (16.86%), organoheterocyclic compounds (15.70%), organic acids and derivatives (13.95%), lipids and lipid‐like molecules (10.47%), benzenoids (6.40%), nucleosides, nucleotides and analogues (4.07%), and alkaloids and derivatives (1.74%; Figure
S5A
). The differential metabolites between TCR and CSR (
n
= 147) also identified to eight classes, including organoheterocyclic compounds (20.14%), organic acids and derivatives (17.99%), phenylpropanoids and polyketides (15.83%), lipids and lipid‐like molecules (11.51%), organic oxygen compounds (10.79%), nucleosides, nucleotides and analogues (10.07%), benzoids (6.47%), and organic nitrogen compounds (2.16%; Figure
S5b
). To verify the effects of different propagation methods on the expression of cane root metabolites, PCA and OPLS‐DA were performed, which revealed distinct clusters for metabolites in TCN and CSN (Figure
5A,B
) and TCR and SSR treatments (Figure
5C,D
). These results suggest that root metabolites are significantly influenced by different propagation methods.

Next, we performed the KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the differential metabolites to identify the key pathways influenced. Three metabolic pathways had effect values >0.3 in both the newly planted (TCN vs. CSN) and ratoon treatments (TCR vs. CSR). The metabolic pathways identified for newly planted treatments were phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis (L‐tryptophan, shikimic acid 3‐phosphate, prephenate, chorismate, L‐tryptophan and 3‐dehydroquinic acid); flavone and flavonol biosynthesis (isoquercitroside, kaempferol‐3‐O‐rutinoside, syringetin, rutin, kaempferol and lampranthin II); and isoflavonoid biosynthesis (Medicarpin, Xenognosin B, Naringenin, Daidzein and Genistein) (Figure

2021
). Flavonols are widely found in the roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds of plants. Moreover, flavonols play important roles in plant growth, development and stress resistance by regulating growth hormone transport, promoting lateral root formation, mediating pollen development, resistance to ultraviolet light and leaf stomatal opening (Falcone Ferreyra et al.,
2012
; Silva et al.,
2016
; Stracke et al.,
2010
).

). Furthermore, amino acids act as osmoregulatory substances to maintain the stability of cell membranes and enhance the scavenging of reactive oxygen species to prevent oxidative damage (Richter et al.,
2015
). The present study demonstrated that alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolisms were upregulated in the TCR treatment group compared with those in the CSR treatment group (Figure
6D
).
In summary, the tissue culture propagation method upregulated the flavone and flavonol biosynthesis and alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolic pathways compared with the conventional propagation method, indicating that the canes grown using the tissue culture propagation method is more conducive to coping with the adverse external environment.

INTRODUCTION
Sugarcane (
Saccharum officinarum
L.) is an annual or perennial tropical and subtropical herb used as the primary raw material for sucrose production (Pang, Dong, et al.,
2021
). China is the third largest sugarcane‐growing country in the world, after Brazil and India (Singh et al.,
2021
). Guangxi is the primary sugarcane production base in China, accounting for 54% of the country's sugar production area and producing 65% of the country's sugar (Tayyab et al.,
2021
; Yang et al.,
2021
). The yield of canes directly affects local economic progress, as the sugar industry plays an important role in the livelihood of several people in China. Furthermore, utilising sugarcane or bagasse to ferment ethanol as a biofuel is considered a suitable alternative to fossil energy sources (Chandel et al.,
2011
). However, excessive fertiliser input and a lack of rational planting practices in fields hinder the improvements in achieving high cane yields and sugar production (Zhou et al.,
2022
).
Sugarcane is mostly propagated asexually because the seeds have a long and slow propagation rate, limiting the use of new and improved seeds. Therefore, research interests in identifying reliable propagation methods are becoming increasingly important for practical applications. In practice, cane stems with buds are widely used for seedling propagation owing to the low cost and simplicity of the method (Pang, Tayyab et al.,
2021
). However, cane stems are also the primary carriers of pests and diseases, which leads to a consequent decline in cane yield and quality (Belete,
2017
). The germination and emergence of cane stems are significantly influenced by several factors, including the part of the cane plant, the chopping method, soil moisture and potassium fertiliser (Sime,
2013
). Furthermore, long‐term stem cultivation can lead to the degradation of the canes and accumulation of pathogens. In contrast, tissue culture‐based methods have been shown to overcome these adversities effectively by producing virus‐free plants (Belete,
2017
; Salokhe,
2021
). For instance, sugarcane plants propagated using tissue culture methods showed resistance to yellow leaf and streak viruses (Fitch et al.,
2001
; Mishra et al.,
2010
). The cane yield has also been shown to be increased by 20%–40% using healthy seedlings obtained through tissue culture (Sbonelo & Sanesh,
2018
). Furthermore, tissue culture seedlings exhibit a stronger tiller capacity and the advantage of saving stems than cane stem propagated seedlings (Kaur & Sandhu,
2015
). Several studies have demonstrated the positive effects of tissue culture methods on cane yield and quality (Tayade et al.,
2021
). However, the mechanisms through which tissue culture methods improve cane yield and quality remain unclear.
Rhizosphere microbes are active life forms that play a crucial role in material recycling and energy metabolism in the soil and are considered the second genome of plants (Bakker & Berendsen,
2022
). They are important in maintaining soil fertility, health and sustainable agricultural production (Mendes et al.,
2011
). Previous studies have shown that soil chemical, physical, and biological processes, and soil microbial community composition can be affected by different agricultural cropping practices with varying fertility properties (Fierer et al.,
2012
; Xun et al.,
2015
). Therefore, we speculated that different planting materials would alter the structure and composition of the rhizosphere microenvironment in sugarcane cropping.
Metabolomics, an emerging discipline following genomics, transcriptomics and proteomics, focuses on qualitative and quantitative analyses of low molecular‐weight metabolites (Fernie & Schauer,
2011
). The metabolome is closer to the phenotype of an organism than to any other histological type. It directly reflects the phenotypic changes in an organism owing to external environmental changes or genetic modifications (Horgan & Kenny,
2011
). Plant secondary metabolites repel pathogens, act as signals for symbiosis between plants and microbes, and alter the microbial community structure (Guerrieri et al.,
2019
). However, the mechanisms via which these metabolites affect soil microbes in sugarcane cropping remain unknown.
We hypothesised that multi‐omics cross‐tabulation analysis (soil microbiome and rhizome metabolomics) could provide insights into the changes in root metabolites and soil microbial community structure in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants obtained using different propagation methods. To test this hypothesis, the present study aims (1) to investigate the changes in cane root metabolites and soil microbial community structure in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants under different propagation methods, (2) to reveal the mechanisms by which tissue culture methods improve cane yield and quality and (3) to reveal the correlation between the abundance of soil microorganisms and root metabolites.
EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE
Study site, experimental design and management
The experiments were conducted at the Experimental Base of Fusui, Chongzuo City, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China (107°55′4″ E, 22°44′56″ N). This location is in a subtropical monsoon climate zone with ample heat, rainfall and sunshine. The average annual temperature and precipitation are approximately 22°C and 1273.6 mm, respectively. The soil type of the experimental site was acidic red loam with the following chemical properties: pH, 5.8; organic matter content, 23.3 g/kg; total nitrogen, 1.7 g/kg; phosphorus, 0.4 g/kg; potassium, 2.7 g/kg. The available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium were 48.7, 12.4 and 66.1 mg/kg, respectively.
Newly planted and ratoon canes (two‐year ratooning) of the “Zhong Tang 3” cultivar were planted in March 2022 and March 2021, respectively. Depending on the method of propagation and types of planting materials used, we designed five treatments as follows: newly planted canes propagated using tissue culture (TCN); newly planted canes propagated using conventional (stem) propagation method (CSN); ratoon canes propagated using tissue culture (TCR); ratoon canes propagated using conventional (stem) propagation method (CSR:); and a barren plot with no sugarcane planting used as a rhizosphere soil control (background, BG).
The experiments were carried out using a randomised block design with 12 experimental plots of 55 m
2
(three plots per treatment). Each plot contained five rows of 10 m length and 1.1 m spacing. In newly planted treatments (TCN and CSN), fertilisers were applied at a 3:7 ratio at the seedling and elongation stages of the crop, respectively, with a fertilisation rate of 300 kg/hm
2
urea (N, 46%), 125 kg/hm
2
KCl (K
2
O, 60%), and 300 kg/hm
2
calcium superphosphate (P
2
O
5
, 18%). The rate of fertilisation in ratoon treatments (TCR and CSR) was 400 kg/hm
2
urea, 225 kg/hm
2
of KCl, and 360 kg/hm
2
calcium superphosphate at a ratio of 4:6 as basal and follow‐up fertilisers, respectively. The intercultural practices, including the weeding, irrigation and pest control, were done using conventional methods.
Root and rhizosphere soil sample collection
Rhizospheric soil samples were randomly collected from the sugarcane cultivation area in November 2022 using the shaking‐off method (Riley & Barber,
1970
). Briefly, three sugarcane plants were selected randomly from each plot. The soil around each plant (~ 60 cm in diameter) was loosened using a sterile shovel. The base of each plant was then held, and the entire plant, along with the surrounding soil, was manually pulled out. The soil adhering to the roots was carefully collected in a sterile sealed bag and placed in a box with ice packs. Additionally, soil samples from the same experimental area without growing sugarcane were randomly collected as BG samples. All samples were transferred to the laboratory as soon as possible and shifted using a 2 mm stainless steel sieve to remove the impurities, like small stones and leaf debris. The shifted material was then stored at −80°C.
Root samples were rinsed with sterile water to remove the soil and attached appendages from the surface. After rinsing, the samples were blotted dry using a sterile filter paper.
Evaluation of soil biological properties
To evaluate the biological properties of soil, we assessed the activities of β‐glucosidase, aminopeptidase, and acid phosphatase using the method described in previous studies (Hayano,
1973
; Ladd,
1972
; Yang et al.,
2021
, respectively). The soil microbial biomass carbon (MBC) and nitrogen were measured using chloroform fumigation and extraction techniques (Brookes et al.,
1985
; Vance et al.,
1987
). The soil microbial biomass P content was determined using the phosphomolybdenum blue colorimetric method (Powlson et al.,
1987
).
Soil microbial diversity analysis
Total DNA was extracted from soil samples using the E.Z.N.A.® Soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio‐tek, Norcross, GA, USA) following the manufacturer's instructions. The integrity of extracted DNA was checked using 1% agarose gel and quantified using a NanoDrop 2000 UV–Vis spectrophotometer (Thermal Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The fungal internal transcribed spacer 1 region was amplified using an ABIGeneAmp® 9700 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) thermal cycler (Applied Biosystems, CA, USA). PCR products were resolved using 2% agar‐gel electrophoresis, purified using the AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (Axygen, USA), and quantified using a quantitative fluorometer (Promega, USA). PCR amplification and sequencing of total DNA extracted from the inter‐root soil samples were performed by Meguiar Biotechnology Ltd. The specific types and sequences of bacteria and fungi are shown in Table
S1
.
LC–MS
‐based soil untargeted metabolomics
The sample (20 mg) was placed in a 2 mL centrifuge tube containing a grinding bead (diameter of 6 mm) and 400 μL of extraction solution (methanol: water = 4:1 [v:v]) containing 0.02 mg/mL of internal standard (L‐2‐chlorophenylalanine) was added for metabolite extraction. The sample solution was then ground for 6 min (−10°C, 50 Hz) in a frozen tissue mill, followed by 30 min of low‐temperature sonication (5°C, 40 kHz). The samples were left at −20°C for 30 min, centrifuged for 15 min (4°C, 13,000 ×
g
), and the supernatant was transferred to an injection vial with an internal cannula for LC–MS analysis. The LC–MS analysis was performed using an ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography‐tandem Fourier transform mass spectrometry system (UHPLC‐Q Exactive, Thermo Fisher Scientific) fitted with an HSS T3 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm; internal diameter, 1.8 μm). The chromatographic conditions were as follows: injection volume, 2 μL; mobile phase A, 95% water +5% acetonitrile (containing 0.1% formic acid); mobile phase B, 47.5% acetonitrile, 47.5% isopropanol, and 5% water (containing 0.1% formic acid); separation gradient: 0–0.1 min, mobile phase B increased from linear 0% to 5%; 0.1–2 min, mobile phase B increased from linear 5% to 25%; 2–9 min, mobile phase B linearity increased from 25% to 100%; 9–13 min, mobile phase B linearity maintained 100%; 13.0–13.1 min, mobile phase B linearity decreased from 100% to 0%; 13.1–29.1 min, the linearity of mobile phase B was maintained at 0% for 16 min; flow rate, 0.40 mL/min; and column temperature, 40°C.
Statistical analysis
Test data were statistically analysed using Microsoft Excel 2019 and SPSS 21.0. The results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation of the mean. The alpha diversity of the bacterial and fungal communities were calculated using Mothur (version 1.30.2,
https://mothur
. org/. com/calculators/; accessed on 9 April 2022). Principal coordinate analysis was performed using the R language (version 3.3.1) tool. For the analysis of microbial community composition and Venn diagrams, OTU tables with 97% similarity were selected and analysed using the R language (version 3.3.1) tool. The pre‐processed metabolite data matrix was subjected to principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS‐DA) using the ‘ropls’ package in R (version 1.6.2). Model stability was assessed using seven cycles of cross‐validation. The selection of significantly different metabolites was determined based on the variable weight values (VIP) and Student's
t
‐test
p
‐values obtained from the OPLS‐DA model; metabolites with VIP >2 and
p
< 0.05 were classified as significantly different metabolites. Using high‐quality KEGG metabolic pathways as the reference, pathway enrichment and topology analyses were performed using Metabolic Analyst 3.0. A heat map was used to correlate the top 15 dominant microorganisms in terms of their abundance with the root metabolites. Online data analysis was performed using the free online Mayobio Cloud Platform (
http://www.majorbio.com
, accessed on August 2, 2022) developed by Mayobio Biomedical Technologies Ltd., Shanghai, China.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Soil enzyme activities and soil microbial biomass
Soil enzymes are highly active organic components that play crucial biochemical roles in decomposing organic matter in soil ecosystems. They are also essential for the soil nutrient cycle (Sowerby et al.,
2005
). Therefore, their activity levels are the indicators of soil microbial diversity and stability changes in soil ecosystem function as well as that of soil health and fertility (Ahamadou et al.,
2009
). In this study, we showed significantly higher β‐glucosidase and aminopeptidase activities in TCN treatment than those in CSN and BG treatments (Table
1
). However, acid phosphatase activity did not differ significantly between the TCN and CSN treatments. In addition, aminopeptidase activity in TCR was significantly higher than those in CSR and BG. The activities of β‐glucosidase and acid phosphatase in the TCR and CSR treatments were significantly higher than those in the BG treatment. However, no significant difference was observed between the TCR and CSR treatments. These results suggest that the soil carbon and nitrogen cycles in the rhizosphere of sugarcane can significantly be improved by the tissue culture propagation method.

Soil bacterial community structure in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under different propagation methods
Soil microbes are crucial in the relationship between plants and the soil. They significantly impact plant growth, productivity, nutrient availability and ecosystem functions (Li et al.,
2019
; Bonkowski & Roy,
2005
). In the newly planted treatments, the Shannon indices of soil bacteria in the sugarcane rhizospheres were not significantly different between TCN and CSN. However, the Ace indices of the soil bacteria in the TCN treatment were significantly higher than those in the CSN and BG treatments (Figure
1A,B
). Significant differences in the soil bacterial composition were detected between the TCN and CSN treatments in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants (Figure
1C
). The numbers of soil bacteria at the OTU level in the TCN, CSN and BG treatments were 3244, 2931 and 2953, respectively. The numbers of unique bacteria in these three treatments were 501, 337 and 351, respectively (Figure
S1A
).

Comparison of soil bacteria in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under different propagation methods. (A) Soil bacterial diversity indices in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under TCN, CSN and BG treatments. (B) Soil bacterial richness indices in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under TCN, CSN, and BG treatments. (C) PCA of soil bacterial communities at the OTU level in the newly planted treatment. (D) Soil bacterial diversity indices in rhizospheres of sugarcane under TCR, CSR, and BG treatments. (E) Soil bacterial richness indices in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under TCR, CSR, and BG treatments. (F) PCA of soil bacterial communities at the OTU level in the ratoon treatment.
In the ratoon cane treatments, the Shannon indices of soil bacteria in the rhizosphere of sugarcane in TCR treatments were significantly higher than those of CSR treatments (Figure
1D
). Moreover, their compositions in TCR, CSR and BG treatments clustered separately (Figure
1D–F
). At the OTU level, the total and unique numbers of soil bacteria in the TCR (3424, 486), CSR (2852, 359) and BG (2953, 318) treatments showed considerable differences (Figure
S1B
). Together, these results suggest the advantages of the tissue culture propagation method on the soil bacterial community structure in the rhizosphere of sugarcane.
Soil microbes play key regulatory roles in suppressing soil‐borne diseases and promoting plant growth (Mendes et al.,
2011
). Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, Acidobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Myxococcus and Patescibacteria were the dominant bacterial phyla in the rhizospheres of sugarcane in the TCN and CSN treatments. Among these, the abundances of Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes and Myxococcus were higher in the TCN treatment than those in the CSN treatment (Figure
2A
). Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LefSe) analysis also showed that Bacteroidetes were significantly enriched in TCN treatment (
p
< 0.05; Figure
S2A
). In addition, Gemmatimonadota and Verrucomicrobiota were the predominant bacterial phyla in the TCN group. Actinobacteria can produce spores in response to harsh environments (Boer et al.,
2005
) and are positively associated with plant residue decomposition, inorganic nitrogen fixation, soil aggregate formation, and plant disease resistance (Zhao et al.,
2016
). An increased abundance of Bacteroidetes indicates high‐quality soil (Kruczyńska et al.,
2023
). Myxococcota are widely distributed in agricultural soils and are important in regulating soil microbial community structure and ecosystem functions (Mohr,
2018
; Wang et al.,
2020
).
FIGURE 2
Soil bacterial compositions in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under different propagation methods. (A, B) Bacterial community composition in TCN, CSN, and BG treatments at the (A) phylum and (B) genus levels. (C, D) Bacterial community composition in TCR, CSR, and BG treatments at the (C) phylum (D) genus levels.
Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, Acidobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Myxococcus, Gemmatimonadota, Patescibacteria, Verrucomicrobiota and Planctomycetota were also identified as dominant bacterial phyla in the rhizospheres of sugarcane in TCR and CSR (Figure
2C
). Compared with the CSR treatment, the proportions of Chloroflexi and Acidobacteria increased with the TCR treatment. Firmicutes, Nitrospirota and Cyanobacteria were the dominant soil bacterial phyla in the rhizosphere of sugarcane under the TCR treatment. Acidobacteria can produce secondary metabolites and antibacterial compounds (Parsley et al.,
2011
; Ward et al.,
2009
). Acidobacteria possess many genes encoding cellulases and hemicelluloses; therefore, it facilitate the degradation of organic residues and material cycling (Kanokratana et al.,
2011
). Nitrospirota suppresses the growth of some disease‐causing fungi, such as
Fusarium graminearum
in wheat and
Fusarium acnes
in strawberries and bananas (Cha et al.,
2016
; Sanguin et al.,
2009
). Moreover, Nitrospirota plays a crucial role in nitrification and nitrogen cycling and helps plant growth (Zhang et al.,
2018
). Cyanobacteria provide organic matter and oxygen to their hosts via biological nitrogen fixation and photosynthesis (Gavazov et al.,
2010
; Zhang, Zhang, et al.,
2011
).
At the genus level, the numbers of soil‐dominant bacterial genera obtained from the TCN, CSN and BG treatments were 17, 17 and 22, respectively (Figure
2B
). Compared to CSN, the ratios of
Bradyrhizobium
,
Sphingomonas
,
Streptomyces
,
Arthrobacter
and
Sinomonas
increased, whereas those of
Burkholderia‐Caballeronia‐Pareaburkholderia
and
Conexibacter
declined in TCN treatment. LefSe analysis demonstrated that
Bradyrhizobium
and
Arthrobacter
were significantly enriched in TCN (
p
< 0.05; Figure
S2A
).
Bradyrhizobium
is a gram‐negative bacteria widely distributed in the soil that forms nodules in plant roots and promotes plant growth and development by fixing atmospheric nitrogen (Favero et al.,
2022
). In addition,
Bradyrhizobium
has a significant inhibitory effect on the growth of pathogenic fungi in the soil, which can reduce the incidence of crop diseases (Basile & Lepek,
2021
).
Sphingomonas
, a group of gram‐negative bacteria, is involved in phosphorus solubilisation functions, degrades soil organic pollutants, and reduces soil toxicity (Li et al.,
2017
).
Streptomyces
is a phosphate‐solubilising soil microorganism that mediates the solubilisation and mineralisation of soil‐insoluble phosphate to a bioavailable form for plants (Abo‐Zai et al.,
2020
). Previous studies have confirmed the efficacy of
Streptomyces
as biofertilisers to improve soil health, reduce barriers to plant succession, and increase plant productivity (Ali et al.,
2021
; Pang et al.,
2022
; Prigigallo et al.,
2023
). Additionally, It can establish a good synergy with
Trichoderma
for biocontrol or plant growth promotion in various crops (Abo‐Zai et al.,
2020
; Ezziyyani et al.,
2007
).
Similarly, the numbers of soil‐dominant bacterial genera obtained from TCR, CSR and BG treatments were 26, 19 and 22, respectively (Figure
2D
). Compared with the CSR treatment, the abundances of
Conexibacter
and
Sinomonas
were enriched in the TCR treatment (
p
< 0.05; Figure
S2B
).
Conexibacter
enhances the resistance of the inter‐root microzone to ecotoxicity and improves microbial community stability in heavy metal‐contaminated soils (Chen et al.,
2022
).
These results indicate that different propagation methods could significantly alter the soil bacterial community composition in the rhizosphere of sugarcane in both newly planted and ratooning systems and that the tissue culture propagation methods recruit more beneficial rhizosphere microorganisms than conventional propagation methods.
Soil fungal community structure in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under different propagation methods
The Shannon indices of soil fungi in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants under TCN treatment were significantly higher than those under CSN and BG treatments. However, no significant difference was observed in the Ace indices of the soil fungi between the TCN and CSN treatments (Figure
3A,B
). Soil fungal composition in the rhizospheres of sugarcane plants differed significantly between TCN and CSN treatments (Figure
3C
). The total numbers of soil fungi at the OTU level in the TCN, CSN and BG treatments were 1502, 1324 and 1190, respectively, and those of unique soil fungi were 528, 325 and 278, respectively (Figure
S2A
).

Comparison of soil fungal diversity in rhizospheres of newly planted and ratooned sugarcanes grown using different propagation methods. (A, B) Soil fungal (A) diversity and (B) richness indices in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under TCN, CSN, and BG treatments. (C) PCA of soil fungal communities at the OTU level in the newly planted treatments. (D, E) Soil fungal (D) diversity and (E) richness indices in rhizospheres of sugarcanes under TCR, CSR, and BG treatments. (F) PCA of soil fungal communities at OTU level obtained in ratoon treatments.
In the ratoon cane treatments, the Shannon indices of soil fungi in the rhizosphere of sugarcane were significantly higher in the TCR treatment than those in the CSR treatment. The Ace and Chao indices of soil fungi were also significantly higher in the TCR and CSR treatments than those in the BG treatment; however, they did not differ significantly between the TCR and CSR treatments (Figure
3D,E
). Moreover, PCA of soil fungal compositions in the rhizosphere of sugarcane plants revealed different clusters in the TCR, CSR and BG treatments (Figure
3F
). This result suggests significant differences in the soil fungal community structure between the TCR and CSR treatments. The numbers of soil fungi obtained in the TCR, CSR and BG treatments at the OTU level were 1502, 1324 and 1190, respectively, whereas those of specific soil fungi were 528, 325 and 278, respectively (Figure
S2B
). Together, these results indicate that compared to conventional propagation, tissue culture propagation can significantly increase the diversity of soil fungi in the rhizosphere of sugarcane.
At the phylum level, Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, unclassified_k_fungi, and Mortierellomycota were the dominant phyla in the rhizospheres of sugarcane under the TCN and CSN treatments (Figure
4A
). Ascomycota was the most abundant fungal phylum in both the TCN and CSN treatments, accounting for 77.36% and 70.83%, respectively. Meanwhile, compared with the CSN treatment, the abundance of Basidiomycota and unclassified_k_Fungi decreased, and that of Mortierellomycota increased in the TCN treatment. Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, unclassified Fungi, and Mortierellomycota were also identified as the dominant fungal phyla in the rhizosphere of sugarcane in TCR and CSR treatments. Among these, the abundance of Mortierellomycota in the TCR treatment was higher in the rhizospheres of sugarcane than that in the CSR treatment (Figure
4C
). Ascomycota is one of the most abundant fungal phyla in soil (Egidi et al.,
2019
) and is a major contributor to soil nutrient turnover and the mineralisation of organic fertilisers (Lazcano et al.,
2013
). Mortierellomycota are also involved in the mineralisation of soil organic matter and enhance crop disease resistance (Shi et al.,
2020
; Zhang, Wu, et al.,
2011
). Mortierella participates in the degradation of plant residues and effectively contributes to the soil carbon cycle (Takashi,
2005
).
FIGURE 4
Soil fungal compositions in rhizospheres of sugarcane under different propagation methods. (A, B) Soil fungal community composition in TCN, CSN and BG treatments at (A) phylum and (B) genus levels. (C, D) Soil fungal community composition in TCR, CSR and BG treatments at (C) phylum and (D) genus levels.
At the genus level, the numbers of soil‐dominant fungal genera in TCN, CSN and BG treatments were 28, 20 and 22, respectively (Figure
4B
). The dominant fungal genera in these treatments comprised
unclassified_k_ Fungi, Saitozyma, Trichoderma, Talaromyces, Chaetomium, unclassified_c_ Sordariomycetes, Fusarium, Penicillium, unclasifed_p_Ascomycota, Mortierella, Trichocladium
and
Coniosporium
. Furthermore, LEfSe analysis revealed significant enrichment of
Exophiala, Rhizoctonia, Chaetosphaeria, Wongia, Sarocladium, Psathyrella, Aspergillus, Monocillium
and
Acremonium
in the rhizospheres of sugarcane in TCN treatment (
p
< 0.05; Figure
S4A
). In contrast,
Talaromyces, Trichoderma
and
Cladophialophora
were significantly enriched in CSN (
p
< 0.05; Figure
S4A
). Previous studies have shown that
Exophiala
spp. have great potential for the bioremediation of hydrocarbon contamination (Woertz et al.,
2001
), including the degradation of benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene (Estévez et al.,
2005
).
Aspergillus
inhibits mycelial growth and spore production in vitro, thereby preventing the development of plant diseases (Kriaa et al.,

CONCLUSIONS
In comparison with the conventional propagation method, soil fertility and health in the rhizospheres of sugarcane can be significantly improved by the tissue culture propagation method. Moreover, the tissue culture method enhanced the abundance of soil‐beneficial microbes, such as
Bradyrhizobium
,
Sphingomonas, Streptomyces, Exophiala
and
Aspergillus
enriched in the rhizospheres of sugarcane, regardless of the seeding newly planted or ratoon canes. Tissue culture propagation upregulated the biosynthesis of flavonoids and flavonols and the metabolism of alanine, aspartate and glutamate significantly in the roots of sugarcane, indicating a positive effect on the composition and function of cane root metabolites. Collectively, these render the tissue culture propagation method as a sustainable method for future sugarcane production.
